#187. Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem

Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis

A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.

The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.

Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced.

Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”

The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.

The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.

Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.

Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.

In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.

Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.

University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.

He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”

#186. Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.

This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”

But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”

Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”

How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”

For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

#184. Reform UK considers pact with Restore Britain to overcome stalling performance in polls

Thursday’s byelection in Castle Bromwich will be latest test for Nigel Farage’s party as rival eats into support

Voters go to the polls in the village of Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands on Thursday in a little-noticed election that is the latest test for Reform at a time when it is particularly vulnerable.

Yet, while it is the Conservatives who are edging ahead in recent polls, the decisive difference could well be the performance of Restore Britain – the hard-right party set up by Rupert Lowe after the MP fell out with Nigel Farage.

Reform has lost no less than five elections since September, on one occasion by as little as two votes, after Restore attracted voters who might otherwise have voted for Farage’s party.

The possibility of offering an electoral pact to Restore is now under discussion among some figures at Reform’s Millbank HQ, the Guardian understands. There is also fervent internal opposition from some who balk at the ethno-nationalism that has found a home in Restore.

“Just take a look at some of the people who have attached themselves to Restore, as well as what some of their people have said about Jews and Muslims in their comments,” said one.

At the same time, and even after an aborted attempt to bury the hatchet between Lowe and Farage, others in Reform are leaving the door open to a reconciliation with Restore at a time when the party needs to find a way to overcome its stalling support.

“There’s an argument that we should be going after Restore and we’ll benefit from that, but there is also one where we work with them … and, to be honest, I don’t know the answer yet,” said one.

One senior Reform source said the idea of a “non-aggression pact” with Restore was in the air and there was a “deal to be done” but was more sceptical about a deeper tie up or merger.

At the same time, other senior Reform figures who are close to Farage are pushing for him to go much further towards a detente with Rupert Lowe, with efforts under way to push them back together.

Among Reform insiders, there is an acknowledgment that Farage is at least as exercised and frustrated about Restore eating into the party’s vote as he is about the investigations into his own financial affairs. One Reform politician said they envisaged Lowe ultimately being readmitted, but that the price would be the exit of Zia Yusuf, who had accused Lowe of assaulting him amid the furore that led to the MP’s suspension from the party.

However, that was before Yusuf this week appeared to praise Lowe in a conversation with the Spectator’s editor, Michael Gove. “Rupert is a force of nature,” said Yusuf, who went on to describe him as a “formidable person” in comments that drew a strikingly warm response from Lowe himself, who tweeted that he appreciated Yusuf’s acknowledgment of Restore’s progress.

“I suspect on policy and trust in politics, Yusuf and I have more in common than the former Tory ministers in Reform’s leadership,” he added.

Last week, there was a public display of Reform working with Restore when the former Tory MPs Andrew Rosindell and Suella Braverman signed an early day motion by Lowe opposing a Liberal Democrat bid to pave the way for census questions to include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as Black English or Asian English.

Even within Restore, and away from the public rhetoric, there is curiosity about the openness of Reform to some form of pact as the speculation about an early general election persists.

“Our offer remains on the table and we are open to negotiating that offer,” said a Restore source, who cited events in the summer when it looked like a reconciliation between Farage and Lowe was in the offing.

“It is Farage and others who have outright rejected it, but the ball is in their court.”

On that occasion, what seemed like tentative moves towards peace broke down amid a fresh row between the two leaders, with Lowe accusing Farage of lying after the latter had said he had reached out but had not heard back.

What remains clear now though is that Restore’s consistent nudging of 5% in serious national polls has taken some in its own ranks and even in Reform – whose leader predicted that its rival “would be lucky to get 1% anywhere” – by surprise. A Restore source said of Reform: “It feels like they’re having a bit of an identity crisis and falling below 20% has clearly given them pause for thought.”

More stark has been the proliferation of Restore branches across the UK – sometimes numbering just a handful of people but in others much larger – and the steady dripfeed of defections from Reform.

Last week, those who joined Lowe at a lavish central London dinner for members of Restore’s “Cromwell Club” for those donating £2,500 a year included Holly Vallance, the estranged wife of Reform’s honorary treasurer Nick Candy, who had frequently been cited as a potential candidate for Farage’s party.

Also there was Charlton Edwards, who was Reform’s treasurer until recently and a figure at the very heart of the courting of donors by Farage’s party.

Aside from the beef between Farage and Lowe – arguably the biggest alpha males on the right – the biggest stumbling block to a pact is the antisemitism within Restore, said one source in Reform, which has made a concerted effort to court the British Jewish community.

“Restore emerged because Rupert was out for revenge and it’s hard to ignore. But there are also things that have been said by people around Restore about Jews, Muslims, that we find deeply uncomfortable,” they said, citing the explicit antisemitism directed towards Restore’s Molly Kingsley online when Lowe unveiled her as his party’s “accountability” spokesperson.

Figures such as Charlie Downes, a Restore election candidate who is often seen by Lowe’s side, have said that only white Christians can truly be British. However, extreme language can also be found in Reform. Last week, the Welsh Senedd member Joe Martin became the first frontline Reform politician to use the term “remigration” – one that originated on the far right and is frequently used by Restore.

Others in Reform, meanwhile, are impressed by the social media strategy of Restore, which has on occasion been backed by Elon Musk.

#183. Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles

A 30-year-old man has been convicted of causing one of the most destructive wildfires in the history of Los Angeles. The verdict came after the case was retried.

A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.

The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).

A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.

While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later amid fierce winds to become the highly destructive Palisades Fire.

The man is set to be sentenced on March 17. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that he could face up to 40 years in prison.

The man was arrested in October 2025, and already faced one trial five months ago that ended with a hung jury. The judge declared a mistrial in June, prompting federal prosecutors to retry the case under modified charges.

Prosecutors said security camera footage and location data from the defendant's cellphone showed he was the only person nearby when ​the January 1 blaze began in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.

At both trials, they characterized the man, a former Uber driver, as a loner who held a deep resentment against society, and particularly the wealthy.

The defense argued that the initial blaze could have been caused by fireworks, while prosecutors said there was no evidence that any had been set off in the area.

In March, the man denied in a court declaration that he had willfully started any fire, though he declined to testify in ⁠his own defense at either trial.

The Palisades blaze erupted almost at the same time as another wildfire that broke out in Eaton Canyon, some 30 miles (48 km) to the east.

That fire, believed to have been ignited by sparks from an electrical transmission tower, killed 19 people and devastated the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.

Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster ever seen in Los Angeles County.

#182. Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”

The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.

Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.

According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”

Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.

Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month,  20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.

There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.

The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

#181. Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal

Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge, often referred to as a mansion tax, will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.

Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 announced she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

When people successfully finish cancer treatment at the hospital they often ring a bell in celebration. “I didn’t ring the bell,” Catherine says in the trailer, speaking to her brother, James Middleton, as they are walking together.

“Maybe this is your ringing the bell,” he says, in reference to her undertaking the Three Peaks challenge and making the programme.

When she completed the challenge in June, 18 months after announcing that the cancer was in remission, she became the first royal to have achieved the feat – climbing Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours, having started on a Saturday evening.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

In the programme, which will be introduced by the presenter Kirsty Young, Catherine talks about how she has learned through her recovery to find “a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty”.

Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said she hoped the documentary “will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges”.

Heal will be shown on BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November and will be available on iPlayer. It will air internationally on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November; Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December; and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December.

#178. US judge jails Indian national in foiled Sikh separatist murder plot

New Delhi has denied any role in the plot to kill Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. Meanwhile, over 200 people have been hospitalized after consuming spurious liquor in Manipur state. DW has more.

Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:

We're logging off today, but we will be back tomorrow with the latest from across India.

Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.

In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.

The IYC said Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.

Manu Jain, who runs the group's social media, told Reuters thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said: "Congress is a party of goons! Goons of Indian Youth Congress are not only vandalized and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad, & also are flaunting it on social media!"

Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav warned foreign companies against getting involved in Indian politics.

The Indian government says it orders takedowns only for content that breaches local laws or threatens public safety or national security. In February, it cut the deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three.

Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the previous six months, saying most were cases where local law required it to restrict content proactively.

Earlier this month, Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta's Facebook $1.3 million for failing to comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election runoff campaign. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's team accused the company of political bias.

India closed day three of the first Test against New Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.

Rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.

"It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul said.

He survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and New Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.

Gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP said.

The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal said.

New Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.

The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.

At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.

At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.

The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.

Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and said the culprits would be arrested soon.

Police said the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.

The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.

A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.

Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.

Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.

Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.

His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.

India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.

Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."

#177. Cold gives way to rain in parts of UK as weather warning issued for south-west England

Flood alerts in place and risk of power cuts as more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday

Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met Office issued a weather warning for south-west England.

It said there will be a slow-moving band of rain moving across Devon and Cornwall, with more than 100mm due to fall on Dartmoor. The warning will be in place from 6am on Sunday until midnight.

The Met Office said there was a risk of power cuts and added that driving conditions could be difficult. There are active flood alerts in the area.

Cold weather health warnings are in place in northern England until Tuesday morning. The lowest temperature this autumn so far was recored on Friday night.

North-west and north-east England, and Yorkshire and the Humber, have had yellow alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency. It suggests there is a risk to vulnerable people and that conditions may put pressure on the health service and people should take care when travelling.

Friday night had the lowest temperature since early January, as Tulloch Bridge in the Highlands recorded -10.6C. It beat this autumn’s record of -8.4C at the same weather station on Thursday.

The Met Office said there could be a widespread frost across the UK on Saturday night, but there will be warmer and largely drier conditions outside south-west England on Sunday.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Matthew Lehnert, said: “Within the warning area, 20-40mm of rain is likely quite widely, but some parts of south Devon and Cornwall could see 60-80mm.

#174. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#173. Suffolk village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plans to house asylum seekers nearby

Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing plans are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’

Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.

After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, said Barnham’s flag would be a stone-curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”.

RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for new developments to house asylum seekers.

A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base.

In Barnham, the plans have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man.

John Bauer, the parish council chair, said this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction.

While in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”.

“We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she said on Friday.

Earlier this month, it was announced construction company Kier would design the new camp at RAF Barnham.

Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone-curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down.

“This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley said. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.”

He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”.

But he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.”

He said the proposed Barnham site had particular issues which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road.

“It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone-curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.”

He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available.

“It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.”

He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

“The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”

#172. A tale of two Nvidias

We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.

Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

#168. Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.

Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.

“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.

It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

#167. 'Killer robots' talks at UN end with no legally binding ban

Countries have agreed to extend discussions over controls on lethal autonomous weapons systems for two years.

United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.

The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop new rules by 2028.

Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.

The conference ended early on Saturday in what campaigners deemed a "weakened" outcome, following several hours of overnight parleying.

Nearly 100 nations had called for negotiations on a legally binding agreement on the systems capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Pope Leo XIV and the Red Cross had also supported a ban on killer robots.

However, countries that have the technology, including arms-producing giants like the ​US, Russia ‌and Israel, were among those opposing the mandate.

Ultimately, the 128 countries  "agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years", the conference's Swiss chair, Julien Thoni, told the media on Saturday.

But while Thoni hailed a multilateral diplomacy delivering "concrete results" even in "today's deeply divided world," rights groups expressed disappointment at the minimal agreement.

"States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument," news agency AFP quoted Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of over 300 organizations, as saying.

"Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document," it added.

The group had earlier said that autonomous weapons systems were already reaching the battlefield and such systems had been tested or deployed, including in the Ukraine war.
